You can start from any cell, and in each step you can move to any of the neighbor cells, in other words, you can go to cells which share an edge with you current cell. Please note that a path of length k means visiting exactly k cells (not necessarily distinct). You CANNOT go off the grid. A path A (of length k) is considered less than a path B (of length k) if after making the ordered lists of the values on the cells that A and B go through (let's call them lst_A and lst_B), lst_A is lexicographically less than lst_B, in other words, there exist an integer index i (1 <= i <= k) such that lst_A[i] < lst_B[i] and for any j (1 <= j < i) we have lst_A[j] = lst_B[j]. It is guaranteed that the answer is unique. Return an ordered list of the values on the cells that the minimum path go through.

def candidate(grid, k):
    n = len(grid)
    path = []
    
    # find the minimum value in the grid
    min_val = min(min(row) for row in grid)
    
    # add the minimum value to the path
    path.append(min_val)
    
    # find the index of the minimum value in the grid
    min_index = [(i, j) for i in range(n) for j in range(n) if grid[i][j] == min_val][0]
    
    # move to the neighbor cell with the minimum value
    for i in range(k - 1):
        min_neighbor = float('inf')
        min_neighbor_index = None
        for x, y in [(min_index[0] - 1, min_index[1]), (min_index[0] + 1, min_index[1]), (min_index[0], min_index[1] - 1), (min_index[0], min_index[1] + 1)]:
            if 0 <= x < n and 0 <= y < n and grid[x][y] < min_neighbor:
                min_neighbor = grid[x][y]
                min_neighbor_index = (x, y)
        path.append(min_neighbor)
        min_index = min_neighbor_index
    
    return path

    # Find the smaller of the two numbers
    smaller = min(a, b)
